newsitem.title: UK: Clinton/Blair to boost special relationship.
newsitem.headline: Clinton/Blair to boost special relationship.

text.p: Britain is set to revive its special relationship with the U.S. on Thursday as President Clinton flies in for the "Tony and Bill" show with new Labour Prime Minister Tony Blair.

Clinton, the first foreign leader to phone Blair after his landslide election victory on May 1, has made no secret of his admiration for Blair whose party had called on the Democrats for electioneering expertise.
Both leaders are already on first name terms and Clinton's London visit has twice been extended -- to a full day -- so that they can socialise more.
Clinton's relationship with Britain's outgoing Conservative Prime Minister John Major had at best been cordial.
He never forgot the help given by the Conservatives to his Republican rival George Bush in the 1992 race for the White House.
Anglo-US relations had plummeted since the heady days when President Ronald Reagan forged a strong personal friendship with "Iron Lady" Margaret Thatcher.
Blair's landslide victory sparked great interest in the United States and he is eager to capitalise on the closer ties.
"He is well aware that the honeymoon won't last forever but that while it does, he intends to use it for Britain's advantage and to stamp Britain on the world map" a spokesman for Blair said.

After 18 years of mistrust between the British Conservative government and the European Union, Blair has sought to make a fresh start with his continental partners, stressing negotiation not confrontation.
On his visit last week to Washington, Britain's new foreign secretary Robin Cook did not see this posing any problems for Anglo-U.S. relations.
He said "Britain as a leading player in Europe would be a more useful partner to the United States than one that was drifting into being a marginalised offshore island."

Blair aides said he would encourage Clinton to keep pressing for an Irish Republican Army ceasefire so that the guerrillas' political arm, Sinn Fein, can gain seats at talks on the future of Northern Ireland.
Similarities abound between the two leaders.
Clinton and Blair, both boyish and handsome, were educated at Oxford University and share a love of rock music. Each is a political pragmatist who ditched dogma on the road to power.
Their wives are both high-flying lawyers determined to be working mothers.

But the London Times disputed their spouses' similarities with one columnist writing: "Apart from their shared membership of the legal profession, Cherie Booth has rather less in common with Hillary Clinton than she does with Socks the White House Cat.
"She will doubtless be relieved when Air Force One and the Clinton crew have departed these shores. Cherie Clinton is no Hillary Clinton and is all the better for it."
